entries.title: Hiroshima survivors warn against Japan's rearmament
entries.summary: On the anniversary of the atomic bombings, survivors and activists tell DW Japan's military buildup risks eroding its longstanding commitment to pacifism.
entries.content:
Japan

Hiroshima survivors warn against Japan's rearmament

August 5, 2026

On the anniversary of the atomic bombings, survivors and activists tell DW Japan's military buildup risks eroding its longstanding commitment to pacifism.

Japan on Thursday commemorates the 81st anniversary of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima.

On August 6, 1945, the US dropped an atomic bomb on the Japanese city of Hiroshima during the last days of World War II, killing close to 80,000 people in the initial blast. Three days later, the US dropped a bomb over Nagasaki.

"Japan adopted a pacifist constitution in reflection on World War II," noted Masako Wada, assistant secretary general of Nihon Hidankyo, or the Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers' Organizations. 

Japan "earned the trust of the international community as a country that promised never to wage a war again," added Wada, who survived the Nagasaki bombing as a 1-year-old.

However, in recent years, Japan has increased defense spending, eased restrictions on weapons exports and expanded the role of its military, citing growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia.

"The current administration is destroying that [trust]," Wada told DW, referring to Japan's recent efforts to pivot away from decades of strict postwar pacifism.

"Japan's recent military buildup is no different from recreating the arms race that led the country toward World War II," said 84-year-old Masashi Ieshima, who survived the Hiroshima bombing at the age of 3.

Survivors warn against rearmament

Ieshima was playing in the entrance of his house, just 1.2 miles (2 km) from the hypocenter, when the blast shattered all the windows in the house, sending shards of glass into his mother.

Seventy years later, he underwent surgery for thyroid cancer, which was officially recognized as an atomic bomb-related illness. His father, who was also exposed to the Hiroshima atomic bombing, died of laryngeal cancer.

"It makes my blood boil to see Japan justify its military buildup and the easing of arms export restrictions over the possibility of a Taiwan conflict," said Ieshima, who serves as the chairman of Toyukai, the Tokyo affiliate of Nihon Hidankyo.

"If Japan continues down this path, it could lead to war. And if another war breaks out, I believe it will be a nuclear war."

The average age of Japan's atomic bomb survivors, known as "hibakusha," has reached almost 87. They face the urgent challenge of passing on their testimony and calls for peace to younger generations, including their children, grandchildren, and supporters.

Takako Nakamura, a second-generation atomic bomb survivor from Nagasaki, began working actively as a family testimony speaker in February 2026, following her career retirement.

"People were killed without a trace, not even their bones remain. That is the true nature of the atomic bomb," the 73-year-old told DW, her voice breaking.

Wada urged people around the world to recognize that the danger of nuclear weapons is "not something in the past, but in front of us right now."

She said she does not want sympathy for survivors, but empathy. "I want people to think of it as their own issue."

Japan pushes for military buildup, non-nuclear principles at risk

On Tuesday, Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the country needs to strengthen its military with a "sense of urgency and crisis" as a new government assessment again highlighted growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

In the preface to Japan's latest annual defense white paper, Koizumi said it was "imperative that Japan further reinforce and transform its defense capabilities with a stronger sense of urgency and crisis than ever before."

The Defense Ministry told DW that Japan must strengthen its defense capabilities to enhance deterrence while maintaining its exclusively defense-oriented policy.

It cited an increasingly severe security environment, including China's military expansion and activities in the East and South China seas and around Taiwan.

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has introduced a series of measures to strengthen Japan's defense capabilities. Her

Her government also relaxed restrictions on arms exports in April 2026, allowing exports of lethal weapons.

It is also considering revising Japan's long-standing commitment to the three non-nuclear principles of not possessing, producing or permitting the entry of nuclear weapons onto Japanese territory.

In November 2025, Takaichi said that a Chinese military attack on Taiwan could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise its legal right to collective self-defense. 

However, the argument that Japan must strengthen its military because China might invade Japan or Taiwan is "not convincing" to the Japanese public, said Koichi Nakano, a professor of political science at Sophia University in Tokyo.

China's military activities, including its maritime expansion, remain limited compared with Russia's war in Ukraine and US attacks on Iran, he told DW.

"Japan is being skillfully drawn into the narrative that it must fall into line with Europe and the US to confront so-called rogue states such as China, North Korea and Russia."

"Japan must responsibly pursue disarmament and establish dialogue," Nakano said. "It must stop demonizing China and recognize it as a country with which meaningful dialogue is possible."

Youth in Japan take to the streets in anti-war protests

Meanwhile, around 27,000 people gathered on July 10 outside the Japanese parliament building in Tokyo, holding colorful illustrated placards with messages such as "No war," and waving glow sticks in the dark.

Reina Tashiro, 36, a member of a civil organization "We Want Our Future," told DW that they aim to "make it as easy as possible for people to take that first step and join a protest."

"It is different from the traditional image of demonstrations, where people raise their fists and shout slogans," Tashiro added. "Our protests may even look stylish."

Nahoko Hishiyama, who has been involved in civic activism for 24 years since the age of 13 and now serves as co-chair of another activist group, pointed out that recent protests have increasingly been led by people in their 20s to 40s, and more women are taking part.

"Japanese women are often said to be too mindful of how others perceive them. In activism, however, that has been turned into a strength, thinking about how to present our message in a way that resonates with the public."

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: A glowing future for nuclear power? Mini reactors explained
entries.summary: Mini reactors are seen as a flexible energy source. Their promise: abundant energy, cheap, clean and climate-friendly with lower water use. But do the numbers add up? We look at what's behind the SMR hype.
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

A glowing future for nuclear power? Mini reactors explained

August 5, 2026

Mini reactors are seen as a flexible energy source. Their promise: abundant energy, cheap, clean and climate-friendly with lower water use. But do the numbers add up? We look at what's behind the SMR hype.

Many politicians and tech companies are now pushing to build new nuclear power plants to meet the world's rapidly growing energy demands. Small reactors — known as Small Modular Reactors, or SMRs — are gaining momentum.

They could be built in less time and come online faster than conventional nuclear power plants. Originally developed to power submarines and aircraft carriers, SMRs largely work the same way as larger reactors.

They contain a nuclear reactor fueled by uranium, which releases enormous amounts of heat through nuclear fission. That heat turns water into steam, and the steam pressure drives turbines that generate electricity.

Companies and startups are working on a wide variety of SMR designs and concepts, but the underlying principle is similar across all of them.

One advantage over conventional nuclear stations is that mini reactors require a maximum of two hectares (around five acres) of land — roughly the size of two soccer fields. By comparison, conventional plants require up to 280 soccer fields, according to the industry.

Why use a modular design for mini nuclear plants?

What makes SMRs particularly attractive is their modular construction. Individual components can be mass-produced as prefabricated modules and pre-assembled off-site — much like a prefab house that simply needs to be put together once it arrives at its location.

Manufacturers promise an extremely short construction time of between one and a half to six years. Large reactors in the US can take anywhere from seven to 10 years to build.

Proponents also argue that modular units could deliver low-emission power to remote regions, where grid infrastructure is often not developed enough to handle the enormous energy output of a large conventional plant.

Those advantages are also shared by renewable energy sources like solar panels and wind turbines — without the risks that come with nuclear power. 

Why less radiation can mean greater risk

The output of mini nuclear reactors is significantly lower than that of conventional nuclear power plants. Depending on the design, SMRs can deliver between 10 and around 200 megawatts of power, while a conventional plant generates between 1,000 and 1,600 MW.

To produce the same amount of energy as the roughly 400 high-capacity reactors currently operating worldwide, tens of thousands of small reactors would need to be built.

SMRs could offer some safety advantages: they contain less radioactive material than large reactors and would be distributed across multiple sites. This means that an accident or military strike resulting in a meltdown would not be as catastrophic as a worst-case scenario at a large reactor. Nevertheless, the consequences of an SMR accident could still be severe.

Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection points out that despite lower radiation levels per reactor, the overall risk posed by mini reactors could be many times higher. Replacing the output of existing nuclear plants with large numbers of smaller ones would require an enormous number of reactors worldwide — and that increases the likelihood that at least one of them will eventually suffer a serious incident.

Nuclear accidents and radiation leaks are extremely rare — but the consequences can be catastrophic. The last major nuclear accident occurred in 2011 at the Fukushima power plant in Japan, following a tsunami. Parts of the region have been contaminated for generations to come, and nearly 170,000 people were forced to flee their homes. 

Extreme efficiency and the dream of radioactive recycling

Part of the hype around some new mini reactors rests on the hope of extracting significantly more energy from the same amount of uranium. Some SMR models — known as "fast reactors" — could theoretically yield 60 to 70 times more energy from uranium than conventional technology, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

But the technology is still in the early stages of development and has so far played only a limited role in IAEA projections. In practice, it has barely been proven in SMRs at all. Only two SMR facilities are currently in operation worldwide — one in China and one in Russia.

Work is also underway on recycling SMR fuel rods, but that process remains largely untested. Most SMR projects continue to rely on the same conventional technology used in traditional reactors.

And the problem of radioactive waste remains unsolved — for both conventional and fast reactors. The risks this poses are already visible: at the Asse facility in Lower Saxony, Germany, a temporary storage site built in the 1970s, hundreds of barrels of intermediate-level radioactive waste are now rusting and beginning to leak. Germany has yet to establish a permanent disposal site.

In fact, no permanent repository for spent fuel or highly radioactive reactor waste is currently in operation anywhere in the world. After 20 years of construction, the Onkalo facility in Finland is set to become the first when it opens in 2026. 

Another problem for nuclear power is growing water scarcity. Recent heat and drought have already forced European nations to curb nuclear output due to for cooling due to low river levels.



Because SMRs are mainly just smaller, simplified versions conventional reactors, they still use water to run and for cooling. While individual units use less water than traditional plants, clustering units could increase overall use, warn experts. Researchers are investigating the use of alternative coolants like molten salts and helium gas for newer designs.

When would SMRs make a climate impact — and at what cost?

Enthusiasm for small reactors runs high in the nuclear community. But what may look promising at first glance is, in many respects, difficult or impossible to back up with solid evidence.

Calculating the costs of a technology still in development is no easy task. Nevertheless, the German Institute for Economic Research estimates that electricity from new mini nuclear plants — even accounting for economies of scale, including construction and manufacturing — will cost at least twice as much per megawatt-hour as the already very affordable electricity generated by solar or wind power. In a worst-case scenario, the cost could be nearly eight times higher.

Adding up all the announcements, plans and strategies of major nations, a few hundred SMRs could come online in China, the US, Europe and India by 2050. But according to Germany's Federal Office for Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection, citing figures from the nuclear industry, production would only become economically viable at a threshold of 3,000 reactors.

The international community has committed to limiting global warmingto well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) by the end of the century. Meeting that target requires large parts of the global economy to become climate-neutral by 2050. The EU aims to reach zero emissions by then; Germany is even targeting net negative CO2 emissions by 2050.

That means climate-friendly nuclear technology would arrive too late to meaningfully limit global warming — and its advantages would be significantly diminished as a result.

What would remain: the radiation risk, and the question of what to do with the radioactive waste.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: My sleep deprivation is your natural short sleep
entries.summary: Every so often we hear of high-ranking politicians or CEOs claiming to get by on very little sleep — some as little as three hours a night. If they’re not natural short sleepers, chances are they’re heading for trouble.
entries.content:
August 5, 2026

Every so often we hear of high-ranking politicians or CEOs claiming to get by on very little sleep — some as little as three hours a night. If they’re not natural short sleepers, chances are they’re heading for trouble.

I've been having trouble sleeping — for as long as forever. Sometimes it's just a feeling. Other times, it's a fact (I know because my watch tells me). But then my watch may be part of the problem. It's constantly reminding me to get to bed on time and accosting me with poor sleep scores. It drives my anxiety through the roof, my heart races and I feel like I can't sleep. But then I still feel fine the next day. Weird.

"When you're sleep deprived, you have poor judgment," said Catia Reis, a sleep researcher at the University of Lisbon, when we spoke.

That might explain my predicament. Because even when I feel fine during the week, I oversleep at the weekend — which is a sure sign of sleep debt, she said.

Reis has studied a variety of sleep-related conditions, including the effects of jet lag and sleep deprivation among athletes. 

One investigation compared levels of sleepiness among patients with sleep apnea — a condition where you stop breathing intermittently through the night — and shift workers, who work against their natural, circadian rhythm. That's our inner clock that tells us when we're wakeful or sleepy. 

She compared the results from both subjective assessments made by participants and objective, clinical tests, and found a "mismatch" in people's ability to assess their own levels of sleepiness the more they were exposed to that very thing: sleepiness.

Basically, the brain stops working. And that should be concerning, given that the brain plays a central role in sleep. 

Sleep or die

When we sleep, the body performs several restorative functions: It removes toxins we have ingested through food or the atmosphere, generates new energy, and is essential for our learning and memory.

"Sleep involves many parts of the brain," said Ying-Hui Fu, a sleep researcher at the University of California San Franscisco. "Almost every disease of the brain, including neurological and psychiatric, [can be linked to] sleep problems."

On average, people need about 7.5-8.5 hours' sleep per night.

But every so often we hear about people in demanding jobs, usually politicians, boasting — or claiming credibility — by saying they rarely sleep more than a few hours; like they're ALWAYS WORKING FOR THE PEOPLE. 

Most recently, it was Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi who reminded us she's slept between zero and three hours per night while in office. 

As a former heavy metal drummer, you might expect a certain level of stamina from the Japanese PM. But while voluntary, habitual (or trained) sleep deprivation — if that's what it is in Takaichi's case — may be an impressive sleep-work-no-life-balance ethic, it's not a good, long-term strategy.

In the best-case scenario, a long-term "sleep debt" can cause your body to accumulate toxins, risking heart or brain disease. In the worst-case scenario, it can be fatal.

"There are only two things more important than sleep for our total health," Fu told DW. "One is air. If we don't have air, we die in a few minutes. The other is water. If we don't have water, we die in a few days. If you don't eat, you can live a couple of months. But if you don't sleep, you can probably only live for a couple of weeks."

And that goes for all animals — "if we don't sleep, we die," she said.

The exception: natural short sleepers

Natural short sleepers are the exception to the rule. They can sleep fewer than six hours per night and not only feel fine, but also actually are fine — healthy, happy and energetic. They appear to have genetic variations that allow them to thrive. Fu cited an 80-year-old natural short sleeper who competed in triathlons. 

Fu and her lab found the first of these variations in the gene DEC2 and published their findings in 2009. Ten years later, they published a paper suggesting that the gene ADRB1 was also linked to Natural Short Sleeper Syndrome. Findings into the genes NPSR1, GRM1, SIK3 followed, and there are others in the pipeline.

We're calling them gene "variations" rather than "mutations" because mutations are often associated with negative health effects. But it appears that Natural Short Sleep does not risk the health issues that habitual short sleepers or sleep deprived people face.

The genes show a range of functions that sleep effects:

  • DEC2: helps regulate sleep/wake duration
  • ADRB1: mediates cardiac and neuronal signaling
  • NPSR1: helps modulate arousal and anxiety
  • GRM1: involved in brain function; may be linked to depression
  • SIK3: plays a role in cell cycle-, metabolic and inflammatory- regulation

Each has taken years of painstaking basic — foundational — research to find and test.

"Every one of us has between 500 to 1,000 unique mutations in our genome. To know which one is causal is very difficult," said Fu.

The impact of better sleep on humanity

The number of known natural short sleepers is small, but Fu says the condition is likely to be more common than research currently suggests.

Most of Fu's findings are limited families that share a gene variation. That's been for a practical, methodological reason: If three members of a family have the same variation and they all appear to be healthy on only four to six hours' sleep, then that gene variation may well be responsible, especially if it's in a gene that is known to be important for healthy sleep function. But it's early days.

"We just know that they perform better and they're healthier. And the most logical explanation for me is that their sleep function is better," said Fu.

Reis is also cautious about the state of research in this area, saying there are still too few studies into natural whort wleepers.

"When we objectively test [habitual short sleepers] and we expand their sleep, we know they improve," said Reis. "But the problem is we don't have enough longitudinal studies with [natural short sleepers]."

Fu would agree. But she said it was a struggle to get the research financed.

"My goal is to help everybody get good sleep. Because if we can help everybody get good sleep, all diseases will drop," said Fu. "The entire spectrum of disease incidence would drop. Can you imagine the impact on humanity?"

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Nepal province legalizes use of medical marijuana
entries.summary: A provincial government in Nepal has legalized the use and growing of marijuana for medical purposes despite a national ban.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal province legalizes use of medical marijuana

August 5, 2026

A provincial government in Nepal has legalized the use and growing of marijuana for medical purposes despite a national ban.

A controversial bill allowing the cultivation and medical use of cannabis, which was endorsed by the chief of Nepal's Gandaki province, took effect on Monday.

However, farmers will required to obtain official permission from the provincial authorities and will be subject to close monitoring.

According to Kathmandu Post, province assembly members from the ruling coalition and opposition parties unanimously passed the legislation.

Gandaki is one of Nepal's seven provinces. The province is home to some of the country's most popular mountains and hiking trails, as well as the resort city of Pokhara.

Marijuana outlawed in Nepal

Gandaki's provincial law sets a precedent in Nepal because it was passed despite a national ban on the cultivation, possession, and use of marijuana.

Possession of marijuana for personal use can result in a one-month jail sentence, while its distribution and sale are punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment, depending on the amount involved.

However, cannabis is native to Nepal, where it is widely used during festivals. Activists have long been campaigning for the government to change the law to permit its cultivation and use.

Marijuana was once deeply embedded in the country's culture and religious traditions. However, in the late 1970s, Nepal joined other nations in outlawing marijuana and expelling the hippies who had flocked there.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Fact check: Did misleading claims about Spain's migration law trigger the Ceuta crisis?
entries.summary: More than 70 people died after thousands of migrants tried to cross from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. The crossings have been linked to misleading claims about a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling.
entries.content:
August 5, 2026

More than 70 people died after thousands of migrants tried to cross from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. The crossings have been linked to misleading claims about a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling.

Misleading social media posts appear to have contributed to a sudden surge in migrant crossings into  Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta. Tens of thousands of people attempted to cross from Morocco in late July. According to authorities, dozens drowned or were killed in crowd-related incidents during the crossings, which triggered a major humanitarian crisis.

European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities blamed the sudden surge in crossings on incorrect information circulating on social media and human traffickers. A recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling on migrant returns became the focus of many of the misleading claims.

The decision was issued several weeks earlier. It ruled that migrants who arrive by sea cannot be subject to the same fast-track deportation procedure applied to people intercepted while crossing physical border infrastructure, such as fences and other official barriers.

Posts on social media claimed that the ruling effectively prevented Spanish authorities from returning migrants who reached Spanish territory by sea, implying that they would be allowed to remain in the country.

The ruling was widely misrepresented online. DW Fact check examined how the claims spread and what the court actually decided.

What was circulating on social media?

Claim: "The Spanish Supreme Court issued a ruling considered one of the most prominent decisions in the migration file, prohibiting the immediate deportation of irregular migrants..."

The claim appeared in Arabic in a Facebook post published on July 13, which described the ruling as "historic." It was one of dozens of similar posts reviewed by DW Fact Check. Some of the accounts spreading the claim were linked to migration-focused pages active on platforms including Telegram, where one profile promoted information about migration opportunities abroad under the slogan "All opportunities for immigration abroad are in your hands."

DW Fact Check also identified numerous examples of smaller and medium-sized accounts sharing posts that used identical or nearly identical wording to the version cited in this article.

DW Fact check: Misleading.

The ruling applies only to migrants arriving by sea who have not crossed a border barrier on their way; it does not apply to all migrants.

Under Spanish law, authorities may carry out immediate returns of people intercepted while breaching official border infrastructure. Migrants who arrive by sea are in a different legal situation because they haven't crossed a barrier. Their cases must be processed individually, with the procedural guarantees the law requires.

The ruling therefore limits the use of immediate returns in these specific cases, but it does not grant migrants an automatic right to remain in Spain. It also allows the government to install physical barriers at sea, which Spain has since done to close what many described as a legal loophole.

Many of the posts reviewed by DW Fact check quoted the ruling without explaining its legal scope. In one example, a TikTok user said “...this law that came out in Spain says it is forbidden to send anyone back if they came swimming to Spain, and it is forbidden for the navy to send them back. This is true...”

The video presented the ruling as a general prohibition on returning migrants who arrive by sea. It did not mention that the Supreme Court’s decision involved the legal procedure for carrying out returns, not a blanket ban on deportation.

DW Fact Check found that this selective interpretation — highlighting the restriction on immediate returns while omitting the broader legal context — appeared repeatedly across a large share of the accounts reviewed.

Can misleading social media claims alone explain the movement toward Ceuta?

The causes of the surge in migrant crossings quickly became the subject of a political dispute between Spain and Morocco.

Spanish officials, including Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, said on July 31 that organized networks had exploited the situation by spreading inaccurate information about the Supreme Court ruling. Madrid also criticized Morocco for failing to prevent thousands of people from reaching the border with Ceuta.

Moroccan authorities rejected accusations that they had deliberately allowed the crossings to happen and said that misleading information on social media caused the mass movement.

According to Lorenzo Piccoli, Assistant Professor of Migration Governance at the European University Institute, the Supreme Court ruling may have played a role in encouraging some people to attempt the crossing, but it could not explain a movement of this scale on its own.

"Even in 2015 and 2016, when up to a million people arrived in Europe, we never saw more than 5,000 or 6,000 in a single day. Here we are talking about 50,000 to 60,000 in one day," Piccoli told DW.

He said it would have been "very difficult" for online claims alone to trigger such a large-scale movement in such a short period of time. "It's very hard to see how this would have happened without some form of coordination or without authorities allowing it to happen," he said.

Piccoli added that there appeared to be a broader political dimension to the crisis, with Morocco potentially not actively causing the movement but failing to prevent it. "There is a recognition that perhaps the Moroccan government did not actively provoke this event, but in some ways it did nothing to avoid it from happening," he said.

entries.title: Hungary's Lake Velence is drying up
entries.summary: Hungary is feeling the heat. The country's third-largest lake is shrinking, the Danube is running low, and soaring temperatures could force the country's only nuclear power plant to shut down.
entries.content:
August 5, 2026

Hungary is feeling the heat. The country's third-largest lake is shrinking, the Danube is running low, and soaring temperatures could force the country's only nuclear power plant to shut down.

A dead fish lies half-decayed on the shore. Its eyes have been picked out by the birds.

Hungary's Lake Velence will likely experience a massive fish kill. That's because oxygen levels in the body of water are too low, according to environmental experts. This means more and more fish will suffocate.

Hungary has seen temperatures soar to 40 degrees Celsius, with barely any rain. This heat is having a major impact on the country's third-largest natural lake.

Its water has never been particularly deep, but the current situation is dire. Water levels have been recorded in Agard, on the southern shore, since 1933. It dropped to a historic low in September 2022, measuring just 53 centimeters. Yet as of today, August 4, the water level has dropped to a mere 29 centimeters (11 inches).

As long as it doesn't rain and temperatures remain hot, the water level will continue to drop every day, by half a centimeter per day on average. The water is currently evaporating at such a fast pace that there may soon be no continuous body of water left, only isolated pools. This could mark a critical tipping point for the lake.

The impact of Hungary's ongoing drought is already clearly visible. The lake has receded by dozens of meters. Ground once covered in water is now so dry that the soil is cracking. The reed belt surrounding the lake, which serves as a habitat for numerous bird species, is now largely rooted in dry soil.

But not all living creatures are suffering under the current conditions: that's evident from a constant hum in the air near the water's edge. As fish and aquatic plants find their habitats shrinking, flies, bacteria, and other decomposers take over, breaking down what the drought leaves behind.

No swimming

The water shortage isn't just changing the lake — it's changing the entire region. Lake Velence is a popular tourist destination, located just 50 kilometers from Hungary's capital, Budapest. It is considered less crowded than nearby Lake Balaton.

But these days, there are barely any visitors. The remaining water has turned a brownish-green and taken on a slightly musty odor. A "No Swimming" sign has been put up, with yellow tape blocking access to the water. Five swimming spots have been closed to the public since July 23.

The Velence municipal government says the beach will only reopen once the lake's water quality improves, though it is unclear when that might happen. The persistent heat and low water levels mean the lake's water is getting warmer and warmer, leading to a growth in bacteria and blue-green algae.

Tourist industry under pressure

The people living around the lake, who make their living in the region's tourist sector, are hard hit by the lake's falling water levels. Today, only one family is visiting the northern beach — not for swimming but sunbathing. There is a water slide, slowly rusting away, with the end of the chute not even reaching the water anymore.

Only one kiosk is open today. A woman is selling langos, Hungary's well-known fried bread, as well as ice cream and lemonade. "The slide hasn't been used for years," the saleswoman tells DW. "It really needs fixing, but who will pay for it when fewer and fewer tourists come here?" Campsites and holiday homes around the lake seem deserted, with many stores closed.

Peggy Barath works in an ice cream shop on Velence Promenade, telling DW, "We've always had a lot of tourists here." She says many visitors were from East Germany, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. But in recent years, their numbers have been dwindling "because of the lake's low water levels."

Peggy says that the ice cream shop now focuses on cyclists rather than tourists looking to swim, as cyclists are undeterred by low water levels.

No long-term solution in sight

Major interventions in the region's water cycle have made the lake more vulnerable to droughts over the years. "The lakeshore has been subject to significant construction activity over the past 15 years," Zoltan Kun, president of the Hungarian Great Lakes and Wetlands Association, tells DW.

"The water management authority has focused on quickly draining excess water from the region rather than storing it using nature-based solutions. And the agricultural industry destroyed our soils, which means they are less able to absorb water."

This isn't the first time Lake Velence has dried up. When this happened in the early 1990s, the lake was replenished with water from various other sources, a solution that proved effective but also expensive and time-consuming. That's why experts are calling for a more sustainable solution today, especially since climate change means more drought periods are expected.

The Zamolyi and Patkai reservoirs could, for instance, be renovated so that water could be stored there during periods of heavy rainfall. During dry spells, this water could then be diverted into Lake Valance.

Yet little has happened so far. In 2021, the government at the time, led by Prime Minister Viktor Orban, rejected a broad investment program for the lake on the grounds that it was too costly. Other projects, however, went ahead.

A new canoe center

Although it has long been clear that water levels drop to a critical level in summer and fall, authorities built a brand-new canoeing center on the north shore between 2021 and 2024, suitable for international competitions. The project cost about 140 million euros in government funds.

Lanes are marked off in the lake with buoys in front of the newly built spectator tower. It's very quiet, like elsewhere along the body of water. Floating docks sit low in the greenish-brown water.

The World University Canoe Championships were supposed to be held here in August, the first major event to be staged at the newly built center. Yet due to persistently low water levels, the event was moved to Szeged, southern Hungary, instead.

This means that for the time being, the Lake Velence facility remains nothing more than an expensive training center.

Nuclear power plant on brink of shutdown

Hungary's ongoing heat wave is being felt all over the country. Water levels of the Danube River have dropped significantly, exposing stretches of dry riverbed around Budapest's Margaret Island. Tourists and locals alike are taking in the unusual sight, snapping photos on a sandbar that has emerged off the island. The low water level has also attracted scrap-metal collectors, who use magnets to pull rusty metal objects from parts of the river that are normally submerged.

The low water level has dramatic consequences. With the exception of a few sightseeing steamboats, boat traffic has almost ceased on the Danube River. Not only that. Paks nuclear power plant, located about 100 kilometers downstream from Budapest, can no longer be cooled with Danube water. The site's electricity output, which covers about half of Hungary's power consumption, has been gradually reduced over the past few days, and it is set to be shut down later this week for the first time ever.

"We are facing a crisis that is beyond our control and putting us to the test," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said at a joint press conference with Interim President Agnes Forsthoffer on Monday. He added that the next five days would be the most critical of the summer of 2026.

Magyar has asked the Hungarian public to conserve electricity. Many companies have agreed to voluntarily reduce their power consumption. Some public buildings and bridges are no longer illuminated at night, and rail freight traffic is suspended between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m.

Hungary faces a very challenging time, with temperatures over 40 degrees Celsius expected over the next days.

This article was translated from German

entries.title: TikTok influencer shot dead during livestream in Mexico
entries.summary: Cesar Gastelum, a Mexican influencer with nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok, was shot dead in the middle of a livestream.
entries.content:
August 5, 2026

Cesar Gastelum, a Mexican influencer with nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok, was shot dead in the middle of a livestream.

Mexican social media influencer Cesar Gastelum was shot and killed on Tuesday while livestreaming with friends outside a fast food restaurant in Culiacan, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, local authorities said.

Gastelum, who had close to 600,000 followers on TikTok, was known for comedy content. He was broadcasting live outside the restaurant with two friends, all reportedly dressed as delivery drivers as part of a challenge for the video. 

What do we know?

During the stream, a motorcycle carrying two people pulled up beside them. Footage from the livestream appeared to show the motorcycle driver shooting at Gastelum's head directly. The broadcast cut out at that moment.

While the video was later taken down by the platform, portions of it continuted to circulate online.

A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastelum's death and said a major security operation was under way. Local television footage showed soldiers and police at the scene, a busy commercial plaza near the state prosecutor's office in Culiacan, while forensic investigators collected evidence.

Initial police reports described the victim as a delivery worker. He was later identified as Gastelum, who local media reported was around 25 years old, after the video and witness accounts helped confirm his identity.

Culiacan at the center of a conflict between rival crime factions

Culiacan, the capital of Sinaloa, has been gripped by violence for the past two years amid an internal power struggle within the region's dominant drug cartel. Local press have reported that several influencers, some allegedly linked to criminal groups, have been killed in Sinaloa in recent years.

The killing echoes the May 2025 death of beauty influencer Valeria Marquez, 23, who was shot while livestreaming on TikTok at the salon where she worked in Zapopan, in Mexico’s western state of Jalisco. Her death was investigated as possible femicide.

Local authorities arrested Ramon Angel Alvarez Ayala, also known as "El R-1," in Jalisco in July. Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch described him as the head of a criminal cell tied to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). Investigators say Alvarez Ayala played a role in Marquez's death and that he financed and directed the November 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Low water levels in the Danube revealing Nazi shipwrecks
entries.summary: There are believed to be about 200 Nazi ships on the floor of the Danube near Prahovo, Serbia. Ferries, tourist boats, and shipping have also become severely restricted due to the drought.
entries.content:
August 5, 2026

There are believed to be about 200 Nazi ships on the floor of the Danube near Prahovo, Serbia. Ferries, tourist boats, and shipping have also become severely restricted due to the drought.

Europe's second-longest river, the Danube, has reached levels so low that sunken German battleships from World War II have emerged from the dried-out riverbed.

Near Prahovo, a Serbian port where the Danube separates the country from Romania, a rusty hull and broken mast has become visible where the Nazis once purposely sunk their own ship to avoid capture by the Russians.

The Serbian government has long sought help from the European Union to remove what are believed to be hundreds of ships, some still laden with weapons, from the river floor. But pinpointing their exact locations without accidentally disturbing the explosives still onboard has been an issue.

Low water levels in the Danube have pushed some power plants in parts of Central and Eastern Europe to the brink of shutting down.

Ferries, tourism boats, and shipping on both the Danube and the Rhine river have been drastically reduced in recent weeks due to the drought.

In recent years, climate change has made lower water levels in Europe's key waterways a recurring issue.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Germany news: Explosive drone defused at Leipzig airport
entries.summary: A German airport was disrupted for hours after an explosive-laden drone was discovered near one of the runways. Investigators are examining a possible political motive. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Explosive drone defused at Leipzig airport

Published August 5, 2026last updated August 5, 2026

A German airport was disrupted for hours after an explosive-laden drone was discovered near one of the runways. Investigators are examining a possible political motive. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Federal police defused an explosive device found on a drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport
  • nvestigators are also examining a second object that hit a cargo aircraft
  • A lightning strike disabled two railway crossing barriers, effectively splitting a German town in two
  • A German employers' organization warns against the watering down of government pension reforms

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, August 5, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section German Interior Minister Dobrindt cuts short holiday over Leipzig drone incident

German Interior Minister Dobrindt cuts short holiday over Leipzig drone incident

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has interrupted his holiday to travel to Leipzig/Halle Airport for security talks following the drone incident.

He is due to meet Saxony Interior Minister Armin Schuster and senior federal and state security officials at the scene, his ministry said.

The head of Germany's federal police Dieter Romann and domestic intelligence chief Sinan Selen are also expected to attend.

Dobrindt is then due to brief the media later in the day.

Schuster earlier warned of a "very serious security incident."

He said state and federal security agencies were working closely together, including Germany's joint center for countering hybrid threats and the federal police's drone defense unit.

Skip next section Explosive-laden drone defused at Leipzig airport

Explosive-laden drone defused at Leipzig airport

German federal police specialists have defused a drone carrying an explosive device after an overnight security incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Officials said the detonator has been removed from an as-yet unidentified explosive device. Authorities say they are not ruling out a political motive, noting that the airport in eastern Germany forms part of the country's critical infrastructure.

The drone carrying the explosive device was found late on Wednesday by an airport employee on the southern runway, according to investigators.

Another flying object later apparently collided with a cargo aircraft, which was taxing on the ground.

Minor damage was discovered after the aircraft landed in Hanover.

Flight operations were initially halted completely after the drone was found.

The northern runway was eventually reopened following a large-scale security sweep overnight, while the southern runway was due to remain closed on Wednesday for maintenance.

Investigators said there was no danger to passengers or airport staff and that passenger flights were not affected.

Skip next section Court rules owner can criticize restaurant online after her dog ate mouse poison there

Court rules owner can criticize restaurant online after her dog ate mouse poison there

A German court has ruled in favor of a woman who publicly criticized a restaurant after her dachshund ate mouse poison while she was dining there.

The Frankfurt Higher Regional Court rejected the restaurant operator's attempt to stop her from describing the incident on Instagram and a review platform.

The woman had visited the restaurant in the Rhine-Main region in spring 2026 with her dachshund, which was lying under a bench inside.

The dog ate mouse bait from a pest-control bait station that had somehow been left accessible and later needed treatment at a veterinary clinic.

That same day, the owner posted about the incident on her own Instagram account and on an account she ran for the dog.

She described what happened as "shocking" and a "massive failure of safety and hygiene."

The court found that readers would understand those remarks as referring to a single incident rather than suggesting the restaurant had permanent or structural hygiene problems.

Judges said the woman was entitled to describe the fact that her dog had been able to reach poison as a "massive" failure, even if her wording was emotional and somewhat exaggerated. They also found that her inaccurate description of the harmful substance as "rat poison" was not so serious a mistake as to warrant restricting her comment.

The statements were therefore protected expressions of opinion, it ruled.

Skip next section German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell

German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell

A court in Hamburg has handed down prison sentences of up to five years to eight alleged members and supporters of the far-right group "Letzte Verteidigungswelle" (Last Line of Defense).

The Higher Regional Court convicted the young defendants on charges including membership in a terrorist organization and attempted murder.

Prosecutors said the group had planned bomb and arson attacks targeting refugees and left-wing activists and had already carried out several attacks.

Seven defendants received juvenile prison sentences ranging from two years and four months to five years. Another was given an 18-month suspended sentence. Three defendants were also convicted of leading the group.

The presiding judge said they had aimed to "create chaos."

Authorities dismantled the group in May last year after investigations spanning several German states.

Prosecutors said members carried out an overnight arson attack on an occupied cultural center in Altdöbern in October 2024 and a pyrotechnic attack on a refugee accommodation center in Schmölln, Thuringia, in January 2025.

No one was injured, although investigators said that was partly down to chance.

The group had also been planning another attack on a refugee center in Senftenberg, Brandenburg.

Several suspects were arrested in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg and Hesse. They were between 14 and 21 years old at the time.

Because some defendants were minors, much of the trial was held behind closed doors. The verdict was delivered publicly.

Skip next section Low water levels in the Danube reveal Nazi shipwrecks

Low water levels in the Danube reveal Nazi shipwrecks

Europe's second-longest river, the Danube, has reached levels so low that sunken German battleships from World War II have emerged from the dried-out riverbed.

Read more about the story here.

Skip next section Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation

Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation

Persistently low water levels on the Rhine could temporarily push Germany's inflation rate up by as much as half a percentage point, economists have warned.

Low water levels are forcing ships to carry much lighter loads, driving up the cost of transporting chemicals, energy supplies and other industrial goods.

Traders said tanker and barge transport costs from Rotterdam to Karlsruhe have climbed to around €150-160 per ton, compared with about €45 at the end of June.

"The German inflation rate could temporarily rise by up to half a percentage point as a result," Berenberg economist Felix Schmidt told the Reuters news agency.

ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski also said shortages and disrupted deliveries could make a wide range of goods more expensive.

"If ships can only be loaded to one-third of capacity or less, correspondingly more ships have to be used, or more expensive alternatives such as trucks or rail," Hamburg Commercial Bank chief economist Cyrus de la Rubia said.

Economists also warned that the disruption could last for months. In previous years, Rhine water levels have often not recovered significantly until November.

Skip next section German employers warn against U-turn on early retirement

German employers warn against U-turn on early retirement

A German employer group has sharply criticized calls to preserve the country's early retirement scheme as debate grows over a proposed overhaul of the pension system.

A government-appointed pension commission presented 33 proposals in June, including abolishing the option of retiring without deductions for people who have paid into the system for particularly long periods.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leadership initially said they wanted to implement the package as closely as possible to the commission's recommendations.

However, several state premiers from both Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union and the SPD have since pushed back against parts of the plan, with particularly strong criticism coming from eastern Germany.

Steffen Kampeter, head of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations, told the Bild newspaper that Germany would not be able to protect jobs and remain competitive without reforming the welfare state.

"I am stunned that central elements of the pension package are already being called into question before they have even been implemented," Steffen Kampeter, head of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations, told the Bild newspaper.

"Anyone who at the same time sticks to retirement from 63 is ignoring the shortage of skilled workers, demographic change and the economic situation," he said.

He warned that watering down the reforms could squander "perhaps the last chance" to make the pension system sustainable as Germany's population ages.

"A future-proof pension system needs more employment, more contributors and solid financing - not ever more promises at the expense of the younger generation," Kampeter said.

Skip next section Unknown object briefly halts flights at Leipzig airport

Unknown object briefly halts flights at Leipzig airport

Flights at Leipzig/Halle Airport were temporarily suspended overnight after an unidentified object was spotted near one of the runways.

Saxony state police said one passenger aircraft and several cargo planes were diverted to other airports during the disruption.

The incident began at around 11:40 p.m. on Tuesday, when an unknown object was seen and another item was later found near the southern runway.

State and federal police are investigating, and a bomb disposal robot was deployed. A police spokesperson told the AFP news agency it was still unclear what the object was.

"There is no danger to the public," the spokesperson said.

Flights resumed at 1:55 a.m. and are now operating via the airport's northern runway, while the southern runway remains partially closed as investigators search for evidence.

The diverted passenger flight was a delayed service from Palma de Mallorca, which was rerouted to Nuremberg.

Skip next section Lightning strike splits town in two

Lightning strike splits town in two

A lightning strike has knocked out barriers at two railway crossings in the Bavarian town of Harburg, effectively splitting the town in two.

Police said the affected roads are the only direct links between the western and eastern parts of Harburg and can no longer be crossed by car.

Residents now face detours of several kilometers, while road crews were working on Wednesday morning to set up alternative routes.

It was unclear when the damage would be repaired. Police said the disruption could continue into the morning rush hour.

A Deutsche Bahn technician has been notified, but repairs may take time because of numerous other weather-related faults.

Until then, the barriers will remain closed.

Police also warned drivers not to use unofficial shortcuts or attempt to drive around the lowered barriers.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

We've been enjoying some sunny weather here on the banks of the parched Rhine River, where the water level is at a record low after a long period of dry weather.

That said, parts of Germany have also seen the odd rumble of thunder.

A lightning strike in Bavaria that kept two railroad crossings jammed closed has cut one town in two, forcing drivers to make lengthy detours.

A storm is also brewing over pension reforms, with an employers' group warning the government not to U-turn on a controversial new policy.

Meanwhile, flights at Leipzig/Halle Airport were briefly suspended overnight after an unidentified object was spotted near one of the runways.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of the things that Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: South Korea: Police raid Starbucks HQ over 'Tank Day' fiasco
entries.summary: Starbucks Korea faced major backlash after being accused of trivializing a 1980 massacre. Police say their internal investigation was not thorough enough.
entries.content:
August 5, 2026

Starbucks Korea faced major backlash after being accused of trivializing a 1980 massacre. Police say their internal investigation was not thorough enough.

Police raided Starbucks' nation headquarters in South Korea on Wednesday, the company confirmed, after a controversial promotional event led to large protests and boycotts of the coffee chain across the country.

"The Seoul police raided the headquarters of Starbucks Korea this morning as part of the ongoing investigation," said a spokesman for the Shinsegae Group, which operates Starbucks Korea.

What was the controversial promotion?

This past May, Starbucks advertised large to-go cups they called "tank tumblers" and seemed to refer to the Gwangju Uprising as "tank day."

On May 18, 1980, the ruling military junta violently put down a pro-democracy protest in the city of Gwangju. At least 165 civilians were killed when the army rolled tanks out into the streets to quell the demonstation.

The Starbucks promotional event also appeared to allude to statements made by the government at the time to deny that they had tortured a student protest leader to death.

The backlash was swift, and led to protest and boycotts against the coffee giant in what is the company's third-largest market after the United States and China.

President Lee Jae Myung also expressed his outrage, and Shinsegae Group chairman Chung Yong-jin and Starbucks Korea CEO Son Jung-hyun resigned following a public apology.

What are police investigating?

Starbucks Korea said it conducted its own internal investigation into the matter and found no evidence of wrongdoing. However, the firm admitted that the inquiry had been hampered by, amongst other things, not being able to compel the people involved in planning the promotion to hand over their phones.

Police told the Yonhap news agency they were looking for evidence that executives knowingly trivialized the 1980 massacre.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar
